entries.bc2d19fa9bd3c9b136ad8c98eb412ddb6b016c91: <div sID="gen24597" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Mark.7" sID="Mark.7"/> <div eID="gen24597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24599" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Christ's dispute with the scribes and Pharisees about eating meat with unwashen hands (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.1-Mark.7.13">ver. 1-13</reference>); and the needful instructions he gave to the people on that occasion, and further explained to his disciples, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.14-Mark.7.23">ver. 14-23</reference>. II. His curing of the woman Canaan's daughter that was possessed, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.24-Mark.7.30">ver. 24-30</reference>. III. The relief of a man that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.31-Mark.7.37">ver. 31-37</reference>.
entries.1c8b812e9642898dfe2f6fb786912bd5a6956b53: <div eID="gen24599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24598" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Traditions of the Elders; The Worst Defilement from Within.</title> <div sID="gen24600" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then came together unto him the Pharisees, and certain of the scribes, which came from Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> And when they saw some of his disciples eat bread with defiled, that is to say, with unwashen, hands, they found fault. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, except they wash <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands oft, eat not, holding the tradition of the elders. <hi type="super">4</hi> And <hi type="italic">when they come</hi> from the market, except they wash, they eat not. And many other things there be, which they have received to hold, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the washing of cups, and pots, brasen vessels, and of tables. <hi type="super">5</hi> Then the Pharisees and scribes asked him, Why walk not thy disciples according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with unwashen hands? <hi type="super">6</hi> He answered and said unto them, Well hath Esaias prophesied of you hypocrites, as it is written, This people honoureth me with <hi type="italic">their</hi> lips, but their heart is far from me. <hi type="super">7</hi> Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching <hi type="italic">for</hi> doctrines the commandments of men. <hi type="super">8</hi> For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, <hi type="italic">as</hi> the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he said unto them, Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition. <hi type="super">10</hi> For Moses said, Honour thy father and thy mother; and, Whoso curseth father or mother, let him die the death: <hi type="super">11</hi> But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; <hi type="italic">he shall be free.</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> And ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother; <hi type="super">13</hi> Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when he had called all the people <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> he said unto them, Hearken unto me every one <hi type="italic">of you,</hi> and understand: 15 There is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him: but the things which come out of him, those are they that defile the man. <hi type="super">16</hi> If any man have ears to hear, let him hear. <hi type="super">17</hi> And when he was entered into the house from the people, his disciples asked him concerning the parable. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he saith unto them, Are ye so without understanding also? Do ye not perceive, that whatsoever thing from without entereth into the man, <hi type="italic">it</hi> cannot defile him; <hi type="super">19</hi> Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats? <hi type="super">20</hi> And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man. <hi type="super">21</hi> For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, <hi type="super">22</hi> Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness: 23 All these evil things come from within, and defile the man. <div eID="gen24600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24601" type="x-p"/> One great design of Christ's coming, was, to set aside the ceremonial law which God made, and to put an end to it; to make way for which he begins with the ceremonial law which men had made, and added to the law of God's making, and discharges his disciples from the obligation of that; which here he doth fully, upon occasion of the offence which the Pharisees took at them for the violation of it. These Pharisees and scribes with whom he had this argument, are said to <hi type="italic">come from Jerusalem</hi> down to Galilee—fourscore or a hundred miles, to pick quarrels with our Saviour there, where they supposed him to have the greatest interest and reputation. Had they come so far to be taught by him, their zeal had been commendable; but to come so far to oppose him, and to check the progress of his gospel, was great wickedness. It should seem that the scribes and Pharisees at Jerusalem pretended not only to a pre-eminence above, but to an authority over, the country clergy, and therefore kept up their visitations and sent inquisitors among them, as they did to John when he appeared, <reference osisRef="John.1.19">John i. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen24601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24602" type="x-p"/> Now in this passage we may observe, <div eID="gen24602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24603" type="x-p"/> I. What the tradition of the elders was: by it all were enjoined to <hi type="italic">wash their hands</hi> before meat; a cleanly custom, and no harm in it; and yet as such to be over-nice in it discovers too great a care about the body, which is <hi type="italic">of the earth;</hi> but they placed religion in it, and would not leave it indifferent, as it was in its own nature; people were at their liberty to do it or not to do it; but they interposed their authority, and commanded all to do it upon pain of excommunication; this they kept up as a <hi type="italic">tradition of the elders.</hi> The Papists pretend to a zeal for the authority and antiquity of the church and its canons, and talk much of councils and fathers, when really it is nothing but a zeal for their own wealth, interest, and dominion, that governs them; and so it was with the Pharisees. <div eID="gen24603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24604" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of the practice of the Pharisees and <hi type="italic">all the Jews,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.3-Mark.7.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. 1. They <hi type="italic">washed their hands oft;</hi> they washed them, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pygme</hi></hi>; the critics find a great deal of work about that word, some making it to denote the frequency of their washing (so we render it); others think it signifies the pains they took in washing their hands; they washed with great care, they washed their hands <hi type="italic">to their wrists</hi> (so some); they lifted up their hands when they were wet, that the water might <hi type="italic">run to their elbows.</hi> 2. They particularly washed before they <hi type="italic">ate bread;</hi> that is, before they sat down to a solemn meal; for that was the rule; they must be sure to wash before they ate the bread on which they begged a blessing. "Whosoever eats the bread over which they recite the benediction, <hi type="italic">Blessed be he that produceth bread,</hi> must wash his hands before and after," or else he was thought to be defiled. 3. They took special care, when they came in <hi type="italic">from the markets,</hi> to wash their hands; from the <hi type="italic">judgment-halls,</hi> so some; it signifies any place of concourse where there were people of all sorts, and, it might be supposed, some heathen or Jews under a ceremonial pollution, by coming near to whom they thought themselves polluted; saying, <hi type="italic">Stand by thyself, come not near me, I am holier than thou,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.5">Isa. lxv. 5</reference>. They say, The rule of the rabbies was—That, if they washed their hands well in the morning, the first thing they did, it would serve for all day, provided they kept alone; but, if they went into company, they must not, at their return, either eat or pray till they had washed their hands; thus the elders gained a reputation among the people for sanctity, and thus they exercised and kept up an authority over their consciences. 4. They added to this the washing of <hi type="italic">cups,</hi> and <hi type="italic">pots,</hi> and <hi type="italic">brazen vessels,</hi> which they suspected had been made use of by heathens, or persons polluted; nay, and the very <hi type="italic">tables</hi> on which they ate their meat. There were many cases in which, by the law of Moses, washings were appointed; but they <hi type="italic">added</hi> to them, and enforced the observation of their own impositions as much as of God's institutions. <div eID="gen24604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24605" type="x-p"/> II. What the practice of Christ's disciples was; they knew what the law was, and the common usage; but they understood themselves so well that they would not be bound up by it: they ate bread with <hi type="italic">defiled,</hi> that is, with <hi type="italic">unwashen, hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.2">v. 2</reference>. Eating with <hi type="italic">unwashen hands</hi> they called eating with <hi type="italic">defiled</hi> hands; thus men keep up their superstitious vanities by putting every thing into an ill name that contradicts them. The disciples knew (it is probable) that the Pharisees had their eye upon them, and yet they would not humour them by a compliance with their traditions, but took their liberty as at other times, and ate bread with <hi type="italic">unwashen</hi> hands; and herein <hi type="italic">their righteousness,</hi> however it might seem to come short, did really <hi type="italic">exceed, that of the scribes and Pharisees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.20">Matt. v. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen24605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24606" type="x-p"/> III. The offence which the Pharisees took at this; They <hi type="italic">found fault</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.2">v. 2</reference>); they censured them as profane, and men of a loose conversation, or rather as men that would not submit to the power of the church, to decree rites and ceremonies, and were therefore rebellious, factious, and schismatical. They brought a complaint against them to their Master, expecting that he should check them, and order them to conform; for they that are fond of their own inventions and impositions, are commonly ready to appeal to Christ, as if he should countenance them, and as if his authority must interpose for the enforcing of them, and the rebuking of those that do not comply with them. They do not ask, Why do not thy disciples <hi type="italic">do as we do?</hi> (Though that was what they meant, coveting to make themselves the standard.) But, Why do not they <hi type="italic">walk according to the tradition of the elders?</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.5">v. 5</reference>. To which it was easy to answer, that, by receiving the doctrine of Christ, they had <hi type="italic">more understanding than all their teachers,</hi> yea <hi type="italic">more than the ancients,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.99-Ps.119.100">Ps. cxix. 99, 100</reference>. <div eID="gen24606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24607" type="x-p"/> IV. Christ's vindication of them; in which, <div eID="gen24607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24608" type="x-p"/> 1. He argues with the Pharisees concerning the authority by which this ceremony was imposed; and <hi type="italic">they</hi> were the fittest to be discoursed with concerning that, who were the great sticklers for it: but this he did not speak of publicly to the multitude (as appears by his <hi type="italic">calling the people</hi> to him, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.14">v. 14</reference>) lest he should have seemed to stir them up to faction and discontent at their governors; but addressed it as a reproof to the persons concerned: for the rule is, <hi type="italic">Suum cuique—Let every one have his own.</hi> <div eID="gen24608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24609" type="x-p"/> (1.) He reproves them for their hypocrisy in pretending to honour God, when really they had no such design in their religious observances (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.6-Mark.7.7">v. 6, 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">They honour me with their lips,</hi> they pretend it is for the glory of God that they impose those things, to distinguish themselves from the heathen; but really <hi type="italic">their heart is far from God,</hi> and is governed by nothing but ambition and covetousness. They would be thought hereby to appropriate themselves as a holy people to the Lord their God, when really it is the furthest thing in their thought. They rested in the outside of all their religious exercises, and their hearts were not right with God in them, and this was worshipping God in vain; for neither was he pleased with such sham-devotions, nor were they profited by them. <div eID="gen24609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24610" type="x-p"/> (2.) He reproves them for placing religion in the inventions and injunctions of their elders and rulers; They <hi type="italic">taught for doctrines the traditions of men.</hi> When they should have been pressing upon people the great principles of religion, they were enforcing the canons of their church, and judged of people's being Jews or no, according as they did, or did not, conform to them, without any consideration had, whether they lived in obedience to God's laws or no. It was true, there were <hi type="italic">divers washings</hi> imposed by the law of Moses (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.10">Heb. ix. 10</reference>), which were intended to signify that inward purification of the heart from worldly fleshly lusts, which God requires as absolutely necessary to our communion with him; but, instead of providing the substance, they presumptuously added to the ceremony, and were very nice in <hi type="italic">washing pots and cups;</hi> and observe, he adds, <hi type="italic">Many other such like things ye do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, Superstition is an endless thing. If one human invention and institution be admitted, though seemingly ever so innocent, as this of washing hands, <hi type="italic">behold, a troop comes,</hi> a door is opened for <hi type="italic">many other such things.</hi> <div eID="gen24610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24611" type="x-p"/> (3.) He reproves them for <hi type="italic">laying aside the commandment of God,</hi> and overlooking that, not urging that in their preaching, and in their discipline conniving at the violation of that, as if that were no longer of force, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, It is the mischief of impositions, that too often they who are zealous for them, have little zeal for the essential duties of religion, but can contentedly see them laid aside. Nay, they <hi type="italic">rejected the commandment of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.9">v. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">He do fairly disannul and abolish the commandment of God;</hi> and even <hi type="italic">by</hi> your traditions <hi type="italic">make the word of God of no effect,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.13">v. 13</reference>. God's statutes shall not only <hi type="italic">lie forgotten,</hi> as antiquated obsolete laws, but they shall, in effect, <hi type="italic">stand repealed,</hi> that their traditions may take place. They were entrusted to expound the law, and to enforce it; and, under pretence of using that power, they violated the law, and dissolved the bonds of it; destroying the text with the comment. <div eID="gen24611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24612" type="x-p"/> This he gives them a particular instance of, and a flagrant one—God commanded children to <hi type="italic">honour their parents,</hi> not only by the law of Moses, but, antecedent to that, by the law of nature; and whoso <hi type="italic">revileth,</hi> or <hi type="italic">speaketh evil of,</hi> father or mother, <hi type="italic">let him die the death,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.10">v. 10</reference>. Hence it is easy to infer, that it is the duty of children, if their parents be poor, to relieve them, according to their ability; and if those children are worthy to die, that curse their parents, much more those that starve them. But if a man will but conform himself in all points to the tradition of the elders, they will find him out an expedient by which he may be discharged from this obligation, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.11">v. 11</reference>. If his parents be in want and he has wherewithal to help them, but has no mind to do it, let him swear by the <hi type="italic">Corban,</hi> that is, by the <hi type="italic">gold of the temple,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">gift upon the altar,</hi> that his parents shall not be profited by him, that he will not relieve them; and, if they ask any thing of him, let him tell them this, and it is enough; as if by the obligation of this wicked vow he had discharged himself from the obligation of God's holy law; thus Dr. Hammond understands it: and it is said to be an ancient canon of the rabbin, That vows take place in things commanded by the law, as well as in things indifferent; so that, if a man make a vow which cannot be ratified without breaking a commandment, the vow must be ratified, and the commandment violated; so Dr. Whitby. Such doctrine as this the Papists teach, discharging children from all obligation to their parents by their monastic vows, and their entrance into religion, as they call it. He concludes, <hi type="italic">Any many such like things do ye.</hi> Where will men stop, when once they have made the word of God give way to their tradition? These eager imposers of such ceremonies, at first only <hi type="italic">made light</hi> of God's commandments <hi type="italic">in comparison</hi> with their traditions, but afterward <hi type="italic">made void</hi> God's commandments, if they stood <hi type="italic">in competition</hi> with them. All this, in effect, Isaiah prophesied of them; what he said of the hypocrites of his own day, was applicable to the scribes and Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.6">v. 6</reference>. Note, When we see, and complain of, the wickedness of the present times, yet we do not <hi type="italic">enquire wisely of that matter,</hi> if we say that all <hi type="italic">the former days were better than these,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Eccl. vii. 10</reference>. The worst of hypocrites and evil doers have had their predecessors. <div eID="gen24612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24613" type="x-p"/> 2. He instructs the people concerning the principles upon which this ceremony was grounded. It was requisite that this part of his discourse should be public, for it related to daily practice, and was designed to rectify a great mistake which the people were led into by their elders; he therefore <hi type="italic">called the people unto him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.14">v. 14</reference>), and bid them <hi type="italic">hear and understand.</hi> Note, It is not enough for the common people to <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> but they must <hi type="italic">understand</hi> what they hear. When Christ would run down the tradition of the Pharisees about washing before meat, he strikes at the opinion which was the root of it. Note, Corrupt customs are best cured by rectifying corrupt notions. <div eID="gen24613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24614" type="x-p"/> Now that which he goes about to set them right in, is, what the pollution is, which we are in danger of being damaged by, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) Not by the <hi type="italic">meat we eat,</hi> though it be eaten with unwashen hands; that is but from without, and goes through a man. But, (2.) It is by the breaking out of the corruption that is in our hearts; the mind and conscience are defiled, guilt is contracted, and we become odious in the sight of God by that which <hi type="italic">comes out</hi> of us; our wicked thoughts and affections, words and actions, these defile us, and these only. Our care must therefore be, to <hi type="italic">wash our heart from wickedness.</hi> <div eID="gen24614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24615" type="x-p"/> 3. He gives his disciples, in private, an explication of the instructions he gave the people. They <hi type="italic">asked</hi> him, when they had him by himself, <hi type="italic">concerning the parable</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.17">v. 17</reference>); for to them, it seems, it was a parable. Now, in answer to their enquiry, (1.) He reproves their dulness; "<hi type="italic">Are ye so without understanding also?</hi> Are ye dull <hi type="italic">also,</hi> as dull as the people that <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> understand, as dull as the Pharisees that <hi type="italic">will not?</hi> Are ye <hi type="italic">so</hi> dull?" He doth not expect they should understand every thing; "But are ye so weak as not to understand <hi type="italic">this?</hi>" (2.) He explains this truth to them, that they might <hi type="italic">perceive</hi> it, and then they would <hi type="italic">believe</hi> it, for it carried its own evidence along with it. Some truths prove themselves, if they be but rightly explained and apprehended. If we understand the spiritual nature of God and of his law, and what it is that is offensive to him, and disfits us for communion with him, we shall soon perceive, [1.] That that which we eat and drink cannot defile us, so as to call for any religious washing; it <hi type="italic">goes into the stomach,</hi> and passes the several digestions and secretions that nature has appointed, and what there may be in it that is defiling is voided and gone; <hi type="italic">meats for the belly, and the belly for meats,</hi> but <hi type="italic">God shall destroy both it and them.</hi> But, [2.] It is that which <hi type="italic">comes out from</hi> the heart, the corrupt heart, that defiles us. As by the ceremonial law, whatsoever (almost) comes out of a man, defiles him (<reference osisRef="Lev.15.2">Lev. xv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.13">Deut. xxiii. 13</reference>), so what comes out from the <hi type="italic">mind</hi> of a man is that which defiles him before God, and calls for a religious washing (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.21">v. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">From within, out of the heart of men,</hi> which they boast of the <hi type="italic">goodness</hi> of, and think is the best part of them, thence that which defiles proceeds, thence comes all the mischief. As a corrupt fountain sends forth corrupt streams, so doth a corrupt heart send forth corrupt reasonings, corrupt appetites and passions, and all those wicked words and actions which are produced by them. Divers particulars are specified, as in Matthew; we had one there, which is not here, and that is, <hi type="italic">false witness-bearing;</hi> but <hi type="italic">seven</hi> are mentioned here, to be added to those we had there. <hi type="italic">First, Covetousnesses,</hi> for it is plural; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">pleonexiai</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">immoderate desires</hi> of more of the wealth of the world, and the gratifications of sense, and still more, still crying, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> Hence we read of a <hi type="italic">heart exercised with covetous practices,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2 Pet. ii. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Wickedness</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">poneriai</hi></hi>; malice, hatred, and ill-will, a desire to do mischief, and a delight in mischief done. <hi type="italic">Thirdly, Deceit;</hi> which is wickedness covered and disguised, that it may be the more securely and effectually committed. <hi type="italic">Fourthly, Lasciviousness;</hi> that filthiness and foolish talking which the apostle condemns; the eye full of adultery, and all wanton dalliances. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">evil eye;</hi> the envious eye, and the covetous eye, grudging others the good we give them, or do for them (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.6">Prov. xxiii. 6</reference>), or grieving at the good they do or enjoy. <hi type="italic">Sixthly, Pride</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyperephania</hi></hi>; exalting ourselves in our own conceit above others, and looking down with scorn and contempt upon others. <hi type="italic">Seventhly, Foolishness</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">aphrosyne</hi></hi>; imprudence, inconsideration; some understand it especially of vainglorious boasting, which St. Paul calls <hi type="italic">foolishness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2 Cor. xi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.19">19</reference>), because it is here joined with <hi type="italic">pride;</hi> I rather take it for that rashness in speaking and acting, which is the cause of so much evil. <hi type="italic">Ill-thinking</hi> is put first, as that which is the spring of all our <hi type="italic">com</hi>missions, and <hi type="italic">unthinking</hi> put last, as that which is the spring of all our <hi type="italic">o</hi>missions. Of all these he concludes (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.23">v. 23</reference>), 1. That they <hi type="italic">come from within,</hi> from the corrupt nature, the carnal mind, the evil treasure in the heart; justly is it said, that the <hi type="italic">inward part is very wickedness,</hi> it must needs be so, when all this comes from within. 2. That they <hi type="italic">defile the man;</hi> they render a man unfit for communion with God, they bring a stain upon the conscience; and, if not mortified and rooted out, will shut men out of the new Jerusalem, into which no <hi type="italic">unclean thing shall enter.</hi>
entries.c8b8f3fb2237efd6dd8e00ce6df132941dbee18b: <div eID="gen24615" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Syrophenician Woman.</title> <div sID="gen24616" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> And from thence he arose, and went into the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and entered into a house, and would have no man know <hi type="italic">it:</hi> but he could not be hid. <hi type="super">25</hi> For a <hi type="italic">certain</hi> woman, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, heard of him, and came and fell at his feet: <hi type="super">26</hi> The woman was a Greek, a Syrophenician by nation; and she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter. <hi type="super">27</hi> But Jesus said unto her, Let the children first be filled: for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto the dogs. <hi type="super">28</hi> And she answered and said unto him, Yes, Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the children's crumbs. <hi type="super">29</hi> And he said unto her, For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter. <hi type="super">30</hi> And when she was come to her house, she found the devil gone out, and her daughter laid upon the bed. <div eID="gen24616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24617" type="x-p"/> See here, I. How <hi type="italic">humbly</hi> Christ was pleased to <hi type="italic">conceal himself.</hi> Never man was so cried up as he was in Galilee, and therefore, to teach us, though not to decline any opportunity of doing good, yet not to be fond of popular applause, he arose from thence, and <hi type="italic">went into the borders</hi> of Tyre and Sidon, where he was little known; and there he entered, not into a synagogue, or place of concourse, but <hi type="italic">into a</hi> private <hi type="italic">house,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">would have no man to know it;</hi> because it was foretold concerning him, <hi type="italic">He shall not strive nor cry, neither shall his voice be heard in the streets.</hi> Not but that he was willing to preach and heal here as well as in other places, but for this he would be sought unto. Note, As there is a time to <hi type="italic">appear,</hi> so there is a time to <hi type="italic">retire.</hi> Or, he would not be known, because he was upon the borders of Tyre and Sidon, among Gentiles, to whom he would not be so forward to show himself as to the tribes of Israel, whose glory he was to be. <div eID="gen24617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24618" type="x-p"/> II. How <hi type="italic">graciously</hi> he was pleased to <hi type="italic">manifest himself,</hi> notwithstanding. Though he would not carry a harvest of miraculous cures into those parts, yet, it should seem, he came on purpose to drop a handful, to let fall this one which we have here an account of. <hi type="italic">He could not be hid;</hi> for, though a candle may be put under a bushel, the sun cannot. Christ was too well known to be long <hi type="italic">incognito—hid,</hi> any where; the oil of gladness which he was anointed with, like ointment of the right hand, would betray itself, and fill the house with its odours. Those that had only heard his fame, could not converse with him, but they would soon say, "This must be Jesus." Now observe, <div eID="gen24618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> 1. The application made to him by a poor woman in distress and trouble. She was a Gentile, a Greek, <hi type="italic">a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel, an alien to the covenant of promise;</hi> she was by extraction a Syrophenician, and not in any degree proselyted to the Jewish religion; she had a <hi type="italic">daughter,</hi> a <hi type="italic">young</hi> daughter, that was possessed <hi type="italic">with the devil.</hi> How many and grievous are the calamities that young children are subject to! Her address was, (1.) Very humble, pressing, and importunate; <hi type="italic">She heard of him,</hi> and <hi type="italic">came, and fell at his feet.</hi> Note, Those that would obtain mercy from Christ, must throw themselves at his feet; must refer themselves to him, humble themselves before him, and give up themselves to be ruled by him. Christ never put any from him, that fell at his feet, which a poor trembling soul may do, that has not boldness and confidence to throw itself into his arms. (2.) It was very particular; she tells him what she wanted. Christ gave poor supplicants leave to be thus free with him; she besought him that he would <hi type="italic">cast forth the devil out of her daughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.26">v. 26</reference>. Note, The greatest blessing we can ask of Christ for our children is, that he would break the power of Satan, that is, the power of sin, in their souls; and particularly, that he would cast forth the <hi type="italic">unclean spirit,</hi> that they may be temples of the Holy Ghost, and he may dwell in them. <div eID="gen24619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24620" type="x-p"/> 2. The discouragement he gave to this address (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.27">v. 27</reference>); He said unto her, "<hi type="italic">Let the children first be filled;</hi> let the Jews have all the miracles wrought for them, that they have occasion for, who are in a particular manner God's chosen people; and let not that which was intended for them, be thrown to those who are not of God's family, and who have not that knowledge of him, and interest in him, which they have, and who are as <hi type="italic">dogs in comparison of them,</hi> vile and profane, and who are as <hi type="italic">dogs to them,</hi> snarling at them, spiteful toward them, and ready to worry them." Note, Where Christ knows the faith of poor supplicants to be strong, he sometimes delights to try it, and put it to the stretch. But his saying, <hi type="italic">Let the children first be filled,</hi> intimates that there was mercy in reserve for the Gentiles, and not far off; for the Jews began already to be surfeited with the gospel of Christ, and some of them had desired him to <hi type="italic">depart out of their coasts.</hi> The children begin to play with their meat, and their leavings, their loathings, would be a feast for the Gentiles. The apostles went by this rule, <hi type="italic">Let the children first be filled,</hi> let the Jews have the first offer; and if their full souls loathe this honeycomb, <hi type="italic">Lo, we turn to the Gentiles!</hi> <div eID="gen24620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24621" type="x-p"/> 3. The turn she gave to this word of Christ, which made against her, and her improvement of it, to make for her, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.28">v. 28</reference>. She said, "<hi type="italic">Yes, Lord,</hi> I own it is true that the <hi type="italic">children's bread</hi> ought not to be cast to the dogs; but they were never denied the <hi type="italic">crumbs</hi> of that bread, nay it belongs to them, and they are allowed a place <hi type="italic">under the table,</hi> that they may be ready to receive them. I ask not for a <hi type="italic">loaf,</hi> no, nor for a <hi type="italic">morsel,</hi> only for a <hi type="italic">crumb;</hi> do not refuse me that." This she speaks, not as undervaluing the mercy, or making light of it in itself, but magnifying the abundance or miraculous cures with which she heard the Jews were feasted, in comparison with which a single cure was but as a crumb. Gentiles do not come in crowds, as the Jews do; <hi type="italic">I come alone.</hi> Perhaps she had heard of Christ's feeding five thousand lately at once, after which, even when they had gathered up the fragments, there could not but be some crumbs left for the dogs. <div eID="gen24621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24622" type="x-p"/> 4. The grant Christ thereupon made of her request. Is she thus humble, thus earnest? For <hi type="italic">this saying, Go thy way,</hi> thou shalt have what thou camest for, <hi type="italic">the devil is gone out of thy daughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.29">v. 29</reference>. This encourages us to <hi type="italic">pray</hi> and not to <hi type="italic">faint,</hi> to continue instant in prayer, not doubting but to prevail at last; the vision at the end shall <hi type="italic">speak, and not lie.</hi> Christ's saying that is <hi type="italic">was done,</hi> did it effectually, as at other times his saying, <hi type="italic">Let it be done;</hi> for (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.30">v. 30</reference>) she <hi type="italic">came to her house,</hi> depending upon the word of Christ, that her daughter was healed, and so she <hi type="italic">found it,</hi> the <hi type="italic">devil was gone out.</hi> Note, Christ can conquer Satan at a distance; and it was not only when the demoniacs <hi type="italic">saw him,</hi> that they yielded to his power (as <reference osisRef="Mark.3.11">ch. iii. 11</reference>), but when they saw him not, for the Spirit of the Lord is not <hi type="italic">bound,</hi> nor <hi type="italic">bounded.</hi> She found her daughter not in any toss or agitation, but very quietly <hi type="italic">laid on the bed,</hi> and reposing herself; waiting for her mother's return, to rejoice with her, that she was so <hi type="italic">finely well.</hi>
entries.4aa83e31b6e87928fae508169abb270c17881fa0: <div eID="gen24622" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cure of a Deaf and Dumb Person.</title> <div sID="gen24623" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And again, departing from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, he came unto the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis. <hi type="super">32</hi> And they bring unto him one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech; and they beseech him to put his hand upon him. <hi type="super">33</hi> And he took him aside from the multitude, and put his fingers into his ears, and he spit, and touched his tongue; <hi type="super">34</hi> And looking up to heaven, he sighed, and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened. <hi type="super">35</hi> And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he charged them that they should tell no man: but the more he charged them, so much the more a great deal they published <hi type="italic">it;</hi> <hi type="super">37</hi> And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well: he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak. <div eID="gen24623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24624" type="x-p"/> Our Lord Jesus seldom staid long in a place, for he knew where his work lay, and attended the changes of it. When he had cured the woman of Canaan's daughter, he had done what he had to do in that place, and therefore presently left those parts, and returned <hi type="italic">to the sea of Galilee,</hi> whereabout his usual residence was; yet he did not come directly thither, but fetched a compass <hi type="italic">through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis,</hi> which lay mostly on the other side Jordan; such long walks did our Lord Jesus take, when he <hi type="italic">went about doing good.</hi> <div eID="gen24624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24625" type="x-p"/> Now here we have the story of a cure that Christ wrought, which is not recorded by any other of the evangelists; it is of one that was <hi type="italic">deaf</hi> and <hi type="italic">dumb.</hi> <div eID="gen24625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24626" type="x-p"/> I. His case was sad, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.32">v. 32</reference>. There were those that brought to him one that was <hi type="italic">deaf;</hi> some think, born deaf, and then he must be dumb of course; others think that by some distemper or disaster he was become deaf, or, at least, thick of hearing; and he had an <hi type="italic">impediment in his speech.</hi> He was <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mogilalos</hi></hi>; some think that he was quite dumb; others, that he could not speak but with great difficulty to himself, and so as scarcely to be understood by those that heard him. He was <hi type="italic">tongue-tied,</hi> so that he was perfectly unfit for conversation, and deprived both of the pleasure and of the profit of it; he had not the satisfaction either of hearing other people talk, or of telling his own mind. Let us take occasion from hence to give thanks to God for preserving to us the sense of hearing, especially that we may be capable of hearing the word of God; and the faculty of speech, especially that we may be capable of speaking God's praises; and let us look with compassion upon those that are deaf or dumb, and treat them with great tenderness. They that brought this poor man to Christ, besought him that he would <hi type="italic">put his hand upon him,</hi> as the prophets did upon those whom they <hi type="italic">blessed</hi> in the name of the Lord. It is not said, They besought him to <hi type="italic">cure him,</hi> but to <hi type="italic">put his hand upon him,</hi> to take cognizance of his case, and put forth his power to do to him as he pleased. <div eID="gen24626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24627" type="x-p"/> II. His cure was solemn, and some of the circumstances of it were singular. <div eID="gen24627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24628" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ <hi type="italic">took him aside from the multitude,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.33">v. 33</reference>. Ordinarily, he wrought his miracles publicly before all the people, to show that they would bear the strictest scrutiny and inspection; but this he did privately, to show that he did not seek his own glory, and to teach us to avoid every thing that savours of ostentation. Let us learn of Christ to be humble, and to do good where no eye sees, but his that is <hi type="italic">all eye.</hi> <div eID="gen24628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24629" type="x-p"/> 2. He used more significant actions, in the doing of this cure, than usual. (1.) He <hi type="italic">put his fingers into his ears,</hi> as if he would <hi type="italic">syringe</hi> them, and fetch out that which stopped them up. (2.) He spit upon his own finger, and then <hi type="italic">touched his tongue,</hi> as if he would moisten his mouth, and so loosen that with which his tongue was tied; these were no causes that could in the least contribute to his cure, but only signs of the exerting of that power which Christ had in himself to cure him, for the encouraging of his faith, and theirs that brought him. The application was all from himself, it was his own <hi type="italic">fingers</hi> that he put into his ears, and his own <hi type="italic">spittle</hi> that he put upon his tongue; for he alone heals. <div eID="gen24629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24630" type="x-p"/> 3. He <hi type="italic">looked up to heaven,</hi> to give his Father the praise of what he did; for he sought his praise, and did his will, and, as Mediator, acted in dependence on him, and with an eye to him. Thus he signified that it was by a divine power, a power her had as the Lord from heaven, and brought with him thence, that he did this; for the <hi type="italic">hearing ear</hi> and the <hi type="italic">seeing eye</hi> the <hi type="italic">Lord has made,</hi> and can remake even <hi type="italic">both of them.</hi> He also hereby directed his patient who could <hi type="italic">see,</hi> though he could not <hi type="italic">hear,</hi> to look up to heaven for relief. Moses with his stammering tongue is directed to look that way (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.11">Exod. iv. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">Who hath made man's mouth? Or who maketh the dumb or deaf, or the seeing or the blind? Have not I the Lord?</hi> <div eID="gen24630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24631" type="x-p"/> 4. He sighed; not as if he found any difficulty in working this miracle, or obtaining power to do it from his father; but thus he expressed his pity for the miseries of human life, and his sympathy with the afflicted in their afflictions, as one that was himself <hi type="italic">touched with the feeling of their infirmities.</hi> And as to this man, he <hi type="italic">sighed,</hi> not because he was loth to do him this kindness, or did it with reluctancy; but because of the many temptations which he would be exposed to, and the sins he would be in danger of, the tongue-sins, after the restoring of his speech to him, which before he was free from. He had better be <hi type="italic">tongue-tied</hi> still, unless he have grace to <hi type="italic">keep his mouth as with a bridle,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen24631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24632" type="x-p"/> 5. He said, <hi type="italic">Ephphatha;</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">Be opened.</hi> This was nothing that looked like <hi type="italic">spell</hi> or <hi type="italic">charm,</hi> such as they used, who had <hi type="italic">familiar spirits,</hi> who <hi type="italic">peeped and muttered,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa. viii. 19</reference>. Christ speaks as one having authority, and power went along with the word. <hi type="italic">Be opened,</hi> served both parts of the cure; "Let the <hi type="italic">ears</hi> be <hi type="italic">opened,</hi> let the <hi type="italic">lips</hi> be <hi type="italic">opened,</hi> let him hear and speak freely, and let the restraint be taken off;" and the effect was answerable (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.35">v. 35</reference>); <hi type="italic">Straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed,</hi> and all was well: and happy he who, as soon as he had his hearing and speech, had the blessed Jesus so near him to converse with. <div eID="gen24632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24633" type="x-p"/> Now this cure was, (1.) A proof of Christ's being the Messiah; for it was foretold that by his power the <hi type="italic">ears of the deaf should be unstopped,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">tongue of the dumb</hi> should be made to <hi type="italic">sing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6">Isa. xxxv. 5, 6</reference>. (2.) It was a specimen of the operations of his gospel upon the minds of men. The great command of the gospel, and grace of Christ to poor sinners, is <hi type="italic">Ephphatha-Be opened.</hi> Grotius applies it thus, that the internal impediments of the mind are removed by the Spirit of Christ, as those bodily impediments were by the word of his power. He <hi type="italic">opens the heart,</hi> as he did Lydia's, and thereby opens the ear to receive the word of God, and opens the mouth in prayer and praises. <div eID="gen24633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24634" type="x-p"/> 6. He ordered it to be kept very private, but it was made very public (1.) It was his humility, that he <hi type="italic">charged them they should tell no man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.7.36">v. 36</reference>. Most men will proclaim their own goodness, or, at least, desire that others should proclaim it; but Christ, though he was himself in no danger of being puffed up with it, knowing that we are, would thus set us an example of self-denial, as in other things, so especially in praise and applause. We should take pleasure in doing good, but not in its being known. (2.) It was their zeal, that, though he charged them to say nothing of it, yet they published it, before Christ would have had it published. But they meant honestly, and therefore it is to be reckoned rather an act of indiscretion than an act of disobedience, <reference osisRef="Mark.7.36">v. 36</reference>. But they that told it, and they that heard it, were <hi type="italic">beyond measure astonished,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hyperperissos</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">more than above measure;</hi> they were exceedingly affected with it, and this was said by every body, it was the common verdict, <hi type="italic">He hath done all things well</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.37">v. 37</reference>); whereas there were those that hated and persecuted him as an <hi type="italic">evil-doer,</hi> they are ready to witness for him, not only that he has done no evil, but that he has done a great deal of good, and has done it well, modestly and humbly, and very devoutly, and all gratis, <hi type="italic">without money and without price,</hi> which added much to the lustre of his good works. He <hi type="italic">maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak;</hi> and that is <hi type="italic">well,</hi> it is well for them, it is well for their relations, to whom they had been a burthen; and therefore <hi type="italic">they</hi> are inexcusable who speak ill of him.  <chapter eID="Mark.7"/> <div eID="gen24634" type="x-p"/>

entries.790f10aae4db0e3a0fb788655431b34ab114a8c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14006"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.7.1-Mark.7.23">Mr 7:1-23</reference>. Discourse on Ceremonial Pollution. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20">Mt 15:1-20</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Matt.15.1-Matt.15.20">Mt 15:1-20</reference>.<div eID="gen27003" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.7.24-Mark.7.37">Mr 7:24-37</reference>. The Syrophoenician Woman and Her Daughter--A Deaf and Dumb Man Healed. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.15.21-Matt.15.31">Mt 15:21-31</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> The Syrophoenician Woman and Her Daughter (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.24-Mark.7.30">Mr 7:24-30</reference>).<div eID="gen27004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> The first words of this narrative show that the incident followed, in point of time, immediately on what precedes it.<div eID="gen27005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14006"/><hi type="bold">24. And from thence he arose, and went into the borders--</hi>or "unto the borders."<div eID="gen27006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Tyre and Sidon--</hi>the two great Phoenician seaports, but here denoting the territory generally, to the frontiers of which Jesus now came. But did Jesus actually enter this heathen territory? The whole narrative, we think, proceeds upon the supposition that He did. His immediate object seems to have been to avoid the wrath of the Pharisees at the withering exposure He had just made of their traditional religion.<div eID="gen27007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and entered into an house, and would have no man know it--</hi>because He had not come there to minister to heathens. But though not "sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.24">Mt 15:24</reference>), He hindered not the lost sheep of the vast Gentile world from coming to Him, nor put them away when they did come--as this incident was designed to show.<div eID="gen27008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he could not be hid--</hi>Christ's fame had early spread from Galilee to this very region (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.8">Mr 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.17">Lu 6:17</reference>). <div eID="gen27009" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a726f28be4a2cf9549c39cfca8d08cfdbe9a819: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14007"/><div sID="gen27010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14007"/><hi type="bold">25. For a certain woman, whose young daughter had an unclean spirit--</hi>or, as in Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">Mt 15:22</reference>), "was badly demonized."<div eID="gen27010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heard of him--</hi>One wonders how; but distress is quick of hearing.<div eID="gen27011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27012" type="x-p"/> and fell at his feet: <div eID="gen27012" type="x-p"/>
entries.1312acb4a1c33b5cf81aec92e8a2993478a63629: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14008"/><div sID="gen27013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14008"/><hi type="bold">26. The woman was a Greek--</hi>that is, "a Gentile," as in the Margin.<div eID="gen27013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a Syrophoenician by nation--</hi>so called as inhabiting the Phoenician tract of Syria. Juvenal uses the same term, as was remarked by Justin Martyr and Tertullian. Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">Mt 15:22</reference>) calls her "a woman of Canaan"--a more intelligible description to his Jewish readers (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.1.30">Jud 1:30</reference>, 32, 33).<div eID="gen27014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter--</hi>"She cried unto Him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David: my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.22">Mt 15:22</reference>). Thus, though no Israelite herself, she salutes Him as Israel's promised Messiah. Here we must go to <reference osisRef="Matt.15.23-Matt.15.25">Mt 15:23-25</reference> for some important links in the dialogue omitted by our Evangelist.<div eID="gen27015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.23">Mt 15:23</reference>:<div eID="gen27016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But he answered her not a word--</hi>The design of this was first, perhaps, to show that He was not sent to such as she. He had said expressly to the Twelve, "Go not into the way of the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.5">Mt 10:5</reference>); and being now among them Himself, He would, for consistency's sake, let it be seen that He had not gone thither for missionary purposes. Therefore He not only kept silence, but had actually left the house, and--as will presently appear--was proceeding on His way back, when this woman accosted Him. But another reason for keeping silence plainly was to try and whet her faith, patience, and perseverance. And it had the desired effect: "She cried after them," which shows that He was already on His way from the place.<div eID="gen27017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And His disciples came and besought Him, saying, Send her away; for she crieth after us--</hi>They thought her troublesome with her importunate cries, just as they did the people who brought young children to be blessed of Him, and they ask their Lord to "send her away," that is, to grant her request and be rid of her; for we gather from His reply that they meant to solicit favor for her, though not for her sake so much as their own.<div eID="gen27018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.24">Mt 15:24</reference>:<div eID="gen27019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">But He answered and said, I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel--</hi>a speech evidently intended for the disciples themselves, to satisfy them that, though the grace He was about to show to this Gentile believer was beyond His strict commission, He had not gone spontaneously to dispense it. Yet did even this speech open a gleam of hope, could she have discerned it. For thus might she have spoken: "I am not SENT, did He say? Truth, Lord, Thou comest not hither in quest of us, but I come in quest of Thee; and must I go empty away? So did not the woman of Samaria, whom when Thou foundest her on Thy way to Galilee, Thou sentest away to make many rich!" But this our poor Syrophoenician could not attain to. What, then, can she answer to such a speech? Nothing. She has reached her lowest depth, her darkest moment: she will just utter her last cry:<div eID="gen27020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.25">Mt 15:25</reference>:<div eID="gen27021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Then came she and worshipped Him, saying, Lord, help me!--</hi>This appeal, so artless, wrung from the depths of a believing heart, and reminding us of the publican's "God be merciful to me a sinner," moved the Redeemer at last to break silence--but in what style? Here we return to our own Evangelist. <div eID="gen27022" type="x-p"/>
entries.3675df338866d6c8f1191ff5ce3a6adf9aa5490f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14009"/><div sID="gen27023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14009"/><hi type="bold">27. But Jesus said unto her, Let the children first be filled--</hi>"Is there hope for me here?" "Filled FIRST?" "Then my turn, it seems, is coming!--but then, 'The CHILDREN first?' Ah! when, on that rule, shall my turn ever come!" But ere she has time for these ponderings of His word, another word comes to supplement it.<div eID="gen27023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for it is not meet to take the children's bread, and to cast it unto the dogs--</hi>Is this the death of her hopes? Nay, rather it is life from the dead. Out of the eater shall come forth meat (<reference osisRef="Judg.14.14">Jud 14:14</reference>). "At evening-time, it shall be light" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.7">Zec 14:7</reference>). "Ah! I have it now. Had He kept silence, what could I have done but go unblest? but He hath spoken, and the victory is mine." <div eID="gen27024" type="x-p"/>
entries.17daf08b98fc3fb791d261ef0a3a0223a6404ded: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14010"/><div sID="gen27025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14010"/><hi type="bold">28. And she answered and said unto him, Yes, Lord--</hi>or, as the same word is rendered in <reference osisRef="Matt.15.27">Mt 15:27</reference>. "Truth, Lord."<div eID="gen27025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet the dogs eat of the children's crumbs--</hi>"which fall from their master's table" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.27">Mt 15:27</reference>). "I thank Thee, O blessed One, for that word! That's my whole case. Not of the children? True. A dog? True also: Yet the dogs under the table are allowed to eat of the children's crumbs--the droppings from their master's full table: Give me that, and I am content: One crumb of power and grace from Thy table shall cast the devil out of my daughter." Oh, what lightning quickness, what reach of instinctive ingenuity, do we behold in this heathen woman! <div eID="gen27026" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a5ccf5bead91be352a46343f24ae15d1b87defb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14011"/><div sID="gen27027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14011"/><hi type="bold">29. And he said unto her--</hi>"O woman, great is thy faith" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.28">Mt 15:28</reference>). As Bengel beautifully remarks, Jesus "marvelled" only at two things--faith and unbelief (see <reference osisRef="Luke.7.9">Lu 7:9</reference>).<div eID="gen27027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For this saying go thy way; the devil is gone out of thy daughter--</hi>That moment the deed was done. <div eID="gen27028" type="x-p"/>
entries.35004e56dfea3fd0f6487526f7cc999017433443: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14012"/><div sID="gen27029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14012"/><hi type="bold">30. And when she was come to her house, she found the devil gone out, and her daughter laid upon the bed--</hi>But Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.28">Mt 15:28</reference>) is more specific; "And her daughter was made whole from that very hour." The wonderfulness of this case in all its features has been felt in every age of the Church, and the balm it has administered, and will yet administer, to millions will be known only in that day that shall reveal the secrets of all hearts.<div eID="gen27029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27030" type="x-p"/> Deaf and Dumb Man Healed (<reference osisRef="Mark.7.31-Mark.7.37">Mr 7:31-37</reference>). <div eID="gen27030" type="x-p"/>
entries.de8a65b92bf6a4c0a8b6510ee3ef8bd805590327: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14013"/><div sID="gen27031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14013"/><hi type="bold">31. And again, departing from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, he came unto the Sea of Galilee--</hi>or, according to what has very strong claims to be regarded as the true text here, "And again, departing from the coasts of Tyre, He came through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee." The manuscripts in favor of this reading, though not the most numerous, are weighty, while the versions agreeing with it are among the most ancient; and all the best critical editors and commentators adopt it. In this case we must understand that our Lord, having once gone out of the Holy Land the length of Tyre, proceeded as far north as Sidon, though without ministering, so far as appears, in those parts, and then bent His steps in a southeasterly direction. There is certainly a difficulty in the supposition of so long a detour without any missionary object: and some may think this sufficient to cast the balance in favor of the received reading. Be this as it may, on returning from these coasts of Tyre, He passed<div eID="gen27031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through the midst of the coasts--</hi>frontiers.<div eID="gen27032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Decapolis--</hi>crossing the Jordan, therefore, and approaching the lake on its east side. Here Matthew, who omits the details of the cure of this deaf and dumb man, introduces some particulars, from which we learn that it was only one of a great number. "And Jesus," says that Evangelist (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.29-Matt.15.31">Mt 15:29-31</reference>), "departed from thence, and came nigh unto the Sea of Galilee, and went up into a mountain"--the mountain range bounding the lake on the northeast, in Decapolis: "And great multitudes came unto Him, having with them lame, blind, dumb, maimed"--not "mutilated," which is but a secondary sense of the word, but "deformed"--"and many others, and cast them down at Jesus' feet; and He healed them: insomuch that the multitude [multitudes] wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see; and they glorified the God of Israel"--who after so long and dreary an absence of visible manifestation, had returned to bless His people as of old (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.7.16">Lu 7:16</reference>). Beyond this it is not clear from the Evangelist's language that the people saw into the claims of Jesus. Well, of these cases Mark here singles out one, whose cure had something peculiar in it. <div eID="gen27033" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a18096cc636b3e7bc284700978b2e6a2ee8c975: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14014"/><div sID="gen27034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14014"/><hi type="bold">32. And they bring unto him one that was deaf ... and they beseech him to put his hand upon him--</hi>In their eagerness they appear to have been somewhat too officious. Though usually doing as here suggested, He will deal with this case in His own way. <div eID="gen27034" type="x-p"/>
entries.17c0445e4640eb9192d7168eaf9e50b1295bc0c2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14015"/><div sID="gen27035" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14015"/><hi type="bold">33. And he took him aside from the multitude--</hi>As in another case He "took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the town" (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.23">Mr 8:23</reference>), probably to fix his undistracted attention on Himself, and, by means of certain actions He was about to do, to awaken and direct his attention to the proper source of relief.<div eID="gen27035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and put his fingers into his ears--</hi>As his indistinct articulation arose from his deafness, our Lord addresses Himself to this first. To the impotent man He said, "Wilt thou be made whole?" to the blind men, "What will ye that I shall do unto you?" and "Believe ye that I am able to do this?" (<reference osisRef="John.5.6">Joh 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.20.32">Mt 20:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.28">9:28</reference>). But as this patient could hear nothing, our Lord substitutes symbolical actions upon each of the organs affected.<div eID="gen27036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he spit and touched his tongue--</hi>moistening the man's parched tongue with saliva from His own mouth, as if to lubricate the organ or facilitate its free motion; thus indicating the source of the healing virtue to be His own person. (For similar actions, see <reference osisRef="Mark.8.23">Mr 8:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.6">Joh 9:6</reference>). <div eID="gen27037" type="x-p"/>
entries.8934cf427f3fa52cec2903512b114b345c00abb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14016"/><div sID="gen27038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14016"/><hi type="bold">34. And looking up to heaven--</hi>ever acknowledging His Father, even while the healing was seen to flow from Himself (see on <reference osisRef="John.5.19">Joh 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen27038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he sighed--</hi>"over the wreck," says Trench, "which sin had brought about, and the malice of the devil in deforming the fair features of God's original creation." But, we take it, there was a yet more painful impression of that "evil thing and bitter" whence all our ills have sprung, and which, when "Himself took our infirmities and bare our sicknesses" (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Mt 8:17</reference>), became mysteriously His own.<div eID="gen27039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> "In thought of these his brows benign,<div eID="gen27040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> Not even in healing, cloudless shine."<div eID="gen27041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27042" type="x-p"/> Keble<div eID="gen27042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and saith unto him, Ephphatha, that is, Be opened--</hi>Our Evangelist, as remarked on <reference osisRef="Mark.5.41">Mr 5:41</reference>, loves to give such wonderful words just as they were spoken. <div eID="gen27043" type="x-p"/>
entries.71aa164fd768aa999c67a2d95204175a6a2b13cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14017"/><div sID="gen27044" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14017"/><hi type="bold">35. And straightway his ears were opened--</hi>This is mentioned first as the source of the other derangement.<div eID="gen27044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain--</hi>The cure was thus alike instantaneous and perfect. <div eID="gen27045" type="x-p"/>
entries.d163e0f2822fb6f066249a1a3716679f816427a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14018"/><div sID="gen27046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14018"/><hi type="bold">36. And he charged them that they should tell no man--</hi>Into this very region He had sent the man out of whom had been cast the legion of devils, to proclaim "what the Lord had done for him" (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.19">Mr 5:19</reference>). Now He will have them "tell no man." But in the former case there was no danger of obstructing His ministry by "blazing the matter" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.45">Mr 1:45</reference>), as He Himself had left the region; whereas now He was sojourning in it.<div eID="gen27046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27047" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the more he charged them, so much the more a great deal they published it--</hi>They could not be restrained; nay, the prohibition seemed only to whet their determination to publish His fame. <div eID="gen27047" type="x-p"/>
entries.36afac9e243a05855ce455accf265c8a7f70a03c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14019"/><div sID="gen27048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14019"/><hi type="bold">37. And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well--</hi>reminding us, says Trench, of the words of the first creation (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.31">Ge 1:31</reference>, Septuagint), upon which we are thus not unsuitably thrown back, for Christ's work is in the truest sense "a new creation,"<div eID="gen27048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he maketh both the deaf to hear and the dumb to speak--</hi>"and they glorified the God of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.31">Mt 15:31</reference>). See on <reference osisRef="Mark.7.31">Mr 7:31</reference>. <chapter eID="Mark.7"/>

entries.3d658e46124690a72953ea2745d9da1761ae157b: <div eID="gen39367" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen39368" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39369" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39369" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen39368" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen39370" type="x-p"/> The Pharisees find fault with the disciples for eating with unwashen hands, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.1-Mar.7.5">Mar 7:1-5</reference>. Christ exposes their hypocrisy, and shows that they had made the word of God of no effect by their traditions, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.6-Mar.7.13">Mar 7:6-13</reference>. He shows what things defile men, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.14-Mar.7.16">Mar 7:14-16</reference>; and teaches his disciples in private, that the sin of the heart alone, leading to vicious practices, defiles the man, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.17-Mar.7.23">Mar 7:17-23</reference>. The account of the Syrophoenician woman, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.24-Mar.7.30">Mar 7:24-30</reference>. He heals a man who was dumb, and had an impediment in his speech, <reference osisRef="Mar.7.31-Mar.7.37">Mar 7:31-37</reference>. <div eID="gen39370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39371" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39372" type="x-p"/> Came from Jerusalem - Probably for the express purpose of disputing with Christ, that they might entangle him in his talk. Malice and envy are never idle - they incessantly hunt the person they intend to make their prey.
entries.0c2da40bee99af869893e131a1108d8b047a050b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39373" type="x-p"/> They found fault - This is wanting in ABEHLV, nineteen others, and several versions: Mill and Bengel approve the omission, and Griesbach rejects the word. If the 3d and 4th verses be read in a parenthesis, the 2d and 5th verses will appear to be properly connected, without the above clause.
entries.b886d2aa6163150d366235ea7c1e0d24878cfc40: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39374" type="x-p"/> Except they wash their hands - πυγμῃ, the hand to the wrist - Unless they wash the hand up to the wrist, eat not. Several translations are given of this word; that above is from Dr. Lightfoot, who quotes a tradition from the rabbins, stating that the hands were to be thus washed. This sort of washing was, and still continues to be, an act of religion in the eastern countries. It is particularly commanded in the Koran, Surat v. ver. 7, "O believers, when ye wish to pray, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows - and your feet up to the ankles." Which custom it is likely Mohammed borrowed from the Jews. The Jewish doctrine is this: "If a man neglect the washing, he shall be eradicated from this world." But instead of πυγμῃ, the fist or hand, the Codex Bezae has πυκνῃ, frequently: and several of the Itala have words of the same signification. Bathing is an indispensable prerequisite to the first meal of the day among the Hindoos; and washing the hands and the feet is equally so before the evening meal. Ward's Customs.
entries.f43344b3ffd184e3810b07d6da41f64e69a1d267: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39375" type="x-p"/> And when they come - This clause is added by our translators, to fill up the sense; but it was probably a part of the original: for εαν ελθωσι is the reading of the Codex Bezae, Vulgate, Armenian, and most of the Itala. The clause in my old MS. Bible is read thus: And thei turninge agein fro chepinge. The words seem essentially necessary to a proper understanding of the text; and, if not admitted on the above authority, they must be supplied in italics, as in our common translation. <div eID="gen39375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39376" type="x-p"/> Except they wash - Or dip; for βαπτισωνται may mean either. But instead of the word in the text, the famous Codex Vaticanus; (B), eight others, and Euthymius, have ῥαντισωνται, sprinkle. However, the Jews sometimes washed their hands previously to their eating: at other times, they simply dipped or plunged them into the water. <div eID="gen39376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39377" type="x-p"/> Of cups - Ποτηριων; any kind of earthen vessels. <div eID="gen39377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39378" type="x-p"/> Pots - Of measures - ξεϚων, from the singular ξεϚης, a measure for liquids, formed from the Latin sextarius, equal to a pint and a half English. See this proved by Wetstein on this place. My old MS. renders it cruetis. <div eID="gen39378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39379" type="x-p"/> Of brazen vessels - Χαλκιων. These, if polluted, were only to be washed, or passed through the fire; whereas the earthen vessels were to be broken. <div eID="gen39379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39380" type="x-p"/> And of tables - Beds, couches - και κλινων. This is wanting in BL, two others, and the Coptic. It is likely it means no more than the forms, or seats, on which they sat to eat. A bed or a couch was defiled, if any unclean person sat or leaned on it - a man with an issue - a leper - a woman with child, etc. As the word βαπτισμους, baptisms, is applied to all these, and as it is contended that this word, and the verb whence it is derived, signify dipping or immersion alone, its use in the above cases refutes that opinion and shows that it was used, not only to express dipping or immersion, but also sprinkling and washing. The cups and pots were washed; the beds and forms perhaps sprinkled; and the hands dipped up to the wrist.
entries.dbb286ea576e30d075deb128eb576c969080cca2: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39381" type="x-p"/> Why walk not thy disciples - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.15.2-Mat.15.9">Mat 15:2-9</reference> (note).
entries.654a1db21a91db903d6cb25d00edad65db974f3e: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen39381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39382" type="x-p"/> Honoreth me - Με τιμᾳ - but the Codex Bezae, and three copies of the Itala, have με αγαπᾳ, loveth me: - the Ethiopic has both readings.
entries.c6c4f4f251963ce6371648ed8459d19599e5c5f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39383" type="x-p"/> Washing of pots and cups, etc. - This whole clause is wanting in BL, five others, and the Coptic: one MS. omits this and the whole of the ninth verse. The eighth verse is not found in the parallel place of <reference osisRef="Mat.15.7-Mat.15.9">Mat 15:7-9</reference>.
entries.ba70622d9990430c3a3d16b965545923344e5139: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39384" type="x-p"/> Full well - Καλως, - a strong irony. How noble is your conduct! From conscientious attachment to your own traditions ye have annihilated the commandments of God! <div eID="gen39384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39385" type="x-p"/> That ye may keep - But στησητε, that ye may establish, is the reading of D, three others, Syriac, all the Itala, with Cyprian, Jerome, and Zeno. Griesbach thinks it should be received instead of the other. God's law was nothing to these men, in comparison of their own: hear a case in point. "Rabba said, How foolish are most men! They observe the precepts of the Divine law, and neglect the statutes of the rabbins!" Maccoth, fol. 22.
entries.988e7d89a9587dca97273635510e255c97145b8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen39385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39386" type="x-p"/> For Moses said, etc. - See all these verses, from this to the 23d, explained Matthew 15:3-20 (note).
entries.1448550c75c631b40cc089dcbdd0a0d39b4b9496: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39387" type="x-p"/> Your tradition - D, later Syriac in the margin, Saxon, and all the Itala but one, add τῃ μωρᾳ, by your Foolish tradition, your foolish law: - Anglo-Saxon.
entries.e814cc53b84e123f3b665b3ff9a66dac54f1fa30: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39388" type="x-p"/> When he had called all the people - But instead of παντα, all, παλιν, again, is the reading of BDL, later Syriac in the margin, Coptic, Ethiopic, Saxon, Vulgate, all the Itala but one. Mill and Griesbach approve of this reading.
entries.387a06c212b64eb27f2970cffe08b75a9398b45c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen39388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39389" type="x-p"/> Into the draught - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.15.17">Mat 15:17</reference> (note). <div eID="gen39389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39390" type="x-p"/> Purging all meats? - For what is separated from the different aliments taken into the stomach, and thrown out of the body, is the innutritious parts of all the meats that are eaten; and thus they are purged, nothing being left behind but what is proper for the support of the body.
entries.401f24e3f3f42b6628d96edd15a6300b10fb001d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen39390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39391" type="x-p"/> Into the borders of Tyre and Sidon - Or, into the country between Tyre and Sidon. I have adopted this translation from Kypke, who proves that this is the meaning of the word μεθορια, in the best Greek writers.
entries.23885e4c77545f119c65bb70e9febdc86b30d81e: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen39391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39392" type="x-p"/> A certain woman - See this account of the Syrophoenician woman explained at large, <reference osisRef="Mat.15.21-Mat.15.28">Mat 15:21-28</reference> (note).
entries.52db189c97802255e1b75aa5d2bbff2e60c72569: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39393" type="x-p"/> The woman was a Greek - Rosenmuller has well observed, that all heathens or idolaters were called Ἑλληνες, Greeks, by the Jews; whether they were Parthians, Medes, Arabs, Indians, or Ethiopians. Jews and Greeks divided the whole world at this period.
entries.87d063d2427397a37e43df0f42394b44f24b1962: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen39393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39394" type="x-p"/> Laid upon the bed - The demon having tormented her, so that her bodily strength was exhausted, and she was now laid upon the couch to take a little rest. The Ethiopic has a remarkable reading here, which gives a very different, and, I think, a better sense. And she found her daughter Clothed, Sitting upon the couch, and the demon gone out.
entries.e4215600cb8befa02b942564a911f1add0800a55: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen39394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39395" type="x-p"/> They bring unto him one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech - Though from the letter of the text, it does not appear that this man was absolutely deprived of speech; for μογιλαλος literally signifies, one that cannot speak plainly - a stammerer; yet it is certain also that the word means a dumb person; and it is likely that the person in question was dumb, because he was deaf; and it is generally found that he who is totally deaf is dumb also. Almost all the versions understand the word thus: and the concluding words seem to confirm this - He maketh both the deaf to hear, and the Dumb, κωφους, to speak.
entries.432730652a51fbc41ae9c90028e61a88c13e45dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen39395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39396" type="x-p"/> And he spit, and touched his tongue - This place is exceedingly difficult. There is scarcely an action of our Lord's life but one can see an evident reason for, except this. Various interpretations are given of it - none of them satisfies my mind. The Abbe Giradeau spiritualizes it thus: - <div eID="gen39396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39397" type="x-p"/> 1. He took him aside from the multitude - When Christ saves a sinner, he separates him from all his old evil companions, and from the spirit and maxims of an ungodly world. <div eID="gen39397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39398" type="x-p"/> 2. He put his fingers in his ears - to show that they could be opened only by the finger, i.e. the power, of God, and that they should be shut to every word and voice, but what came from him. <div eID="gen39398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39399" type="x-p"/> 3.
