Spitting out he touched his tongue - to show that his mental taste and relish should be entirely changed: that he should detest those things which he before esteemed, and esteem those which he before hated. <div eID="gen39399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39400" type="x-p"/> 4. Looking up to heaven - to signify that all help comes from God, and to teach the new convert to keep continually looking to and depending upon him. <div eID="gen39400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39401" type="x-p"/> 5. He groaned - to show the wretched state of man by sins and how tenderly concerned God is for his present and eternal welfare; and to intimate that men should seek the salvation of God in the spirit of genuine repentance, with strong crying and tears. <div eID="gen39401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39402" type="x-p"/> 6. He said, Be opened - Sin is a shutting of the ears against the words of God; and a tying of the tongue, to render it incapable of giving God due praise. But when the all-powerful grace of Christ reaches the heart, the ear is unstopped, and the man hears distinctly - the tongue is unloosed, and the man speaks correctly. <div eID="gen39402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39403" type="x-p"/> After all, it is possible that what is attributed here to Christ belongs to the person who was cured. I will give my sense of the place in a short paraphrase. <div eID="gen39403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39404" type="x-p"/> And Jesus took him aside from the multitude: and [the deaf man] put his fingers into his ears, intimating thereby to Christ that they were so stopped that he could not hear; and having spat out, that there might be nothing remaining in his mouth to offend the sight when Christ should look at his tongue, he touched his tongue, showing to Christ that it was so bound that he could not speak: and he looked up to heaven, as if to implore assistance from above: and he groaned, being distressed because of his present affliction, and thus implored relief: for, not being able to speak, he could only groan and look up, expressing by these signs, as well as he could, his afflicted state, and the desire he had to be relieved. Then Jesus, having compassion upon him, said, Be opened: and immediately his ears were opened, so that he could hear distinctly; and the impediment to his speaking was removed, so that he spake properly. The original will admit of this interpretation; and this, I am inclined to believe, is the true meaning of this otherwise (to me and many others) unaccountable passage.
entries.f893381d04488e62331b292e55b14f4531e82487: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen39404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39405" type="x-p"/> Ephphatha - Ethphathach, Syriac. It is likely that it was in this language that our Lord spoke to this poor man: and because he had pronounced the word Ephphathach with peculiar and authoritative emphasis, the evangelist thought proper to retain the original word; though the last letter in it could not be expressed by any letter in the Greek alphabet.
entries.3b683411217ab9f645b2368377eb43872b308e27: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen39405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39406" type="x-p"/> He spake plain - Ορθως, distinctly, without stammering. One MS. has, And he spoke, praising God. There is no doubt of this: but the evangelist, I think, did not write these words.
entries.b2e4739a57a26f718ee07899ddf5338713cc8a1f: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen39406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39407" type="x-p"/> Tell no man - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.4">Mat 8:4</reference> (note). This miracle is not mentioned by any other of the evangelists. Another proof that Mark did not abridge Matthew. For a practical review of the different important subjects of this chapter, see Matthew 15:1-39 (note), and particularly the observations at the end.
entries.047b5a514bb1e7a77d5c8b5fa6cedb82d2d008cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen39407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39408" type="x-p"/> He hath done all things well - This has been, and ever will be, true of every part of our Lord's conduct. In creation, providence, and redemption he hath done all things well. The wisest philosophers are agreed that, considering creation as a whole, it would be impossible to improve it. Every thing has been made in number, weight, and measure; there really is nothing deficient, nothing redundant; and the good of the creature seems evidently more consulted than the glory of the Creator. The creature's good is every where apparent; but to find out how the Creator is glorified by these works requires the eye of the philosopher. And as he has done all things well in creation, so has he in providence: here also every thing is in number, weight, measure, and time. As creation shows his majesty, so providence shows his bounty. He preserves every thing he has made; all depend upon him; and by him are all things supported. But how glorious does he appear in the work of redemption! How magnificent, ample, and adequate the provision made for the salvation of a lost world! Here, as in providence, is enough for all, a sufficiency for each, and an abundance for eternity. He loves every man, and hates nothing that he has made; nor can the God of all grace be less beneficent than the Creator and Preserver of the universe.  <chapter eID="Mark.7"/> <div eID="gen39408" type="x-p"/>

entries.c31fba9bead4031aa502b36038a6dffebfa7c9fb:
Verse 3. Except they wash their hands oft. The word oft means frequently, often. The word translated oft has been rendered various ways. Some have said that it means "up to the wrist;" unless they wash their hands up to the wrist. Others have said, "up to the elbow." There is evidence that the Pharisees had some such foolish rule as this about washing, and it is likely that they practised it faithfully, But the word probably means, diligently, accurately, carefully. Unless they wash their hands carefully, or according to rule, etc.

entries.db88e72661463dc79041a92e92e0e50463913a8e:
Verse 4. Market. This word means either the place where provisions were sold, or the place where men were convened for any purpose. In this place it probably means the former.

Except they wash. In the original, "Except they baptize." In this place it does not mean to immerse the whole body, but the hands only. There is no evidence that the Jews washed their whole bodies every time they came from market. It is probable they washed as a mere ceremony; and often, doubtless, with the use of a very small quantity of water.

The washing of cups. In the Greek, the baptism of cups.

Cups. Drinking vessels. Those used at their meals.

Pots. Measures of liquids. Vessels made of wood, used to hold wine, vinegar, etc.

Brasen vessels. Vessels made of brass, used in cooking or otherwise. These, if much polluted, were commonly passed through the fire; if slightly polluted, they were washed. Earthen vessels, if defiled, were usually broken.

Tables. This word means, in the original, beds or couches. It refers not to the tables on which they ate, but to the couches on which they reclined at their meals. Mt 23:6. These were supposed to be defiled when any unclean or polluted person had reclined on them; and they deemed it necessary to purify them with water. The word baptism is here used--in the original, the baptism of tables; but as it cannot be supposed that couches were entirely immersed in water, the word baptism, here, must denote some other application of water, by sprinkling or otherwise, and shows that the term is used in the sense of washing in any way. If the word here is used, as is clear, to denote anything except entire immersion, it may be elsewhere; and baptism is lawfully performed without immersing the whole body in water.

entries.4796e8ef2c72b4f0f703bdc83c6081f465f5e2d9: Verse 18. Cannot defile him. Cannot render his soul polluted; cannot make him a sinner, so as to need this purifying as a religious observance.
entries.52b42e39ddc1e9867db2a2afae8bed6e260faac2:
Verse 19. Entereth not into his heart. Does not reach or affect the mind, the soul, and consequently cannot pollute it. Even if it should affect the body, yet it cannot the soul, and consequently cannot need to be cleansed by a religious ordinance. The notions of the Pharisees, therefore, are not founded in reason, but are mere superstition.

The draught. The sink, the vault.

Purging all meats, The word purging, here, means to purify, to cleanse. What is thrown out of the body is the innutrious part of the food taken into the stomach, and leaving only that which is proper for the support of life; and it cannot, therefore, defile the soul.

All meats. All food; all that is taken into the body to support life. The meaning is, that the economy or process by which life is supported, purifies or renders nutritious all kinds of food. The unwholesome parts are separated, and the wholesome only are taken into the system. This agrees with all that has since been discovered of the process of digestion, and of the support of life. The food taken into the stomach is, by the gastric juice, converted into a thick pulp, called chyme. The nutritious part of this is conveyed into small vessels and changed into a milky substance called chyle. This is changed into blood, and the blood conveys nutriment and support to all parts of the system. The useless parts of the food are thrown off.

entries.3f365059fb8dda8fa9e58ac32d67539171ad2ef6:

entries.c505cd48b1ceafeca92256ab16de8c9458b0f5b8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.7.24" sID="gen100058" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.24">Mark 7:24</reference></hi><hi type="italic">. He wished that no man should know it.</hi> We must attend to this circumstance, which is mentioned by Mark, that when Christ came to that place, he did not erect his banner, but endeavored to remain concealed for a time, in that obscure situation, like a private individual. Mark speaks according to the ordinary perception of the flesh; for, although Christ by his divine Spirit foresaw what would happen, yet so far as he was the minister and ambassador of the Father, he kept himself, as his human nature might have led us to expect, within the limits of that calling which God had given him; and in that respect it is said that what he wished, <hi type="italic">as man, </hi>he was unable to accomplish. Meanwhile, this occurrence, as I have said, tends powerfully to condemn the Jews, who—though they boasted that they were the heirs of the covenant of the Lord, his peculiar people, and a royal priesthood—were blind and deaf when Christ, with a loud voice and with the addition of miracles, offered to them the promised redemption; while this woman, who had no relationship with the children of Abraham, and to whom, at first sight, the covenant did not at all belong, came of her own accord to Christ, without having heard his voice or seen his miracles.<div eID="gen100059" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100058" osisID="Mark.7.24" type="section"/>
entries.c1b7c0db003ae82ebfe5ebc82f221309c72b6467: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.7.32" sID="gen100101" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.32">Mark 7:32</reference>. </hi><hi type="italic">And they bring to him one who was deaf.</hi> The reason why <hi type="italic">they implored him to lay his hands upon him</hi> may be learned from passages which we have already considered; for the <hi type="italic">laying on of hands</hi> was a solemn symbol of consecration, <note n="423"> <div sID="gen100103" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour dedier et eonsacrer les personnes</foreign>;” — “for dedicating and con-secrating persons.”<div eID="gen100103" type="x-p"/> </note> and by means of it, the gifts of the Holy Spirit were also bestowed. And there is no doubt that this ceremony was frequently used by Christ; so that those men requested nothing but what they knew that he had been formerly in the habit of doing. On the present occasion, Christ employs other symbols; for he puts his <hi type="italic">spittle </hi>on the <hi type="italic">tongue </hi>of the <hi type="italic">dumb man, and puts his fingers into his ears.</hi> The <hi type="italic">laying on of hands</hi> would of itself have been sufficiently efficacious, and even, without moving a finger, he might have accomplished it by a single act of his will; but it is evident that he made abundant use of outward signs, when they were found to be advantageous. Thus, by touching the <hi type="italic">tongue </hi>with <hi type="italic">spittle</hi>, he intended to point out that the faculty of speech was communicated by himself alone; and by <hi type="italic">putting his finger into the ears</hi>, he showed that it belonged to his office to pierce the ears of the deaf. There is no necessity for having recourse to allegories; and we find that those who have amused themselves with ingenious discussions on this subject, are so far from bringing forward any thing of real value, that they tend rather to hold up the Scriptures to ridicule. Readers of sobriety and judgment will be satisfied with this single instruction, that we obtain from Christ, in answer to our prayers, both speech and hearing; for he pours his energy into our tongues, and pierces our ears with his fingers.<div eID="gen100102" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100101" osisID="Mark.7.32" type="section"/>
entries.def594415fe8ec76e64847257107cf03784f68fd: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.7.33" sID="gen100104" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">33. </hi><hi type="italic">And when he had taken him aside from the multitude.</hi> This was done, partly to afford to those who were ignorant, and not yet sufficiently qualified for becoming witnesses, an opportunity of perceiving at a distance the glory of his Divine nature, and partly that he might have a better opportunity of pouring out earnest prayer. When he <hi type="italic">looked up to heaven and sighed</hi>, it was an expression of strong feeling; and this enables us to perceive the vehemence of his love towards men, for whose miseries he feels so much compassion. Nor can it be doubted, that by conveying the spittle from his own mouth to the mouth of another, and by <hi type="italic">putting his fingers into his ears,</hi> he intended to manifest and express the same feeling of kindness. Yet that he has supreme power to remove all our defects, and restore us to health, is proclaimed by him when he simply orders the tongue and ears <hi type="italic">to be opened; </hi>for it was not without a good reason that Mark inserted that Chaldaic word, (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐφφαθά</foreign>) <hi type="italic">Ephphatha</hi>,<hi type="italic"> be opened</hi>, but to testify the divine power of Christ. Among other fooleries with which baptism has been debased by foolish men, the ceremony used by our Lord is turned into a piece of buffoonery; and this instance shows us that there is no end to licentiousness, when men wantonly change at their own pleasure the mysteries of God.<div eID="gen100105" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100104" osisID="Mark.7.33" type="section"/>
entries.198b599c7cc6ab849e825af81cbffdc50f26870e:
36. Then he enjoined them not to tell it to any person. Many commentators torture these injunctions to an opposite meaning, as if Christ had purposely excited them to spread abroad the fame of the miracle; but I prefer a more natural interpretation which I have formerly stated,
Harmony, vol. 1. p. 374.
that Christ only intended to delay the publication of it till a more proper and convenient time. I have no doubt, therefore, that their zeal was unseasonable, when, though enjoined to be silent, they were in haste to speak. We need not wonder that men unaccustomed to the doctrine of Christ are carried away by immoderate zeal, when it is not called for. Yet what they unwisely attempted to do, was made by Christ to promote his own glory; for not only was the miracle made known, but the whole of that district, in despising the Author of heavenly gifts, was rendered inexcusable.
entries.d66aa8a6daf64926a7fa826b872bf565c0e78c3e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.37" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.7.37" sID="gen100109" type="section"/> <div sID="gen100110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">37. </hi><hi type="italic">He hath done all things well.</hi> Matthew, after collecting many miracles, concludes by saying that <hi type="italic">the multitudes wondered, and glorified the God of Israel; </hi>that is, because God, taking unusual methods of illustrating his power, had called up the remembrance of his covenant. But the words of Mark contain perhaps an implied contrast; for the reports concerning Christ were various, and the word <hi type="italic">multitude </hi>or <hi type="italic">crowd </hi>(<foreign xml:lang="el">ὄχλος</foreign>) may be intended to mean that it was only wicked and malicious persons who slandered his actions, since all that he did was so far from exposing him to calumny that it deserved the highest praise. But we know, and it is what nature teaches us, that nothing is more unjust than to make the bestowal of favors an occasion of envy and ill-will.<div eID="gen100110" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.7.37" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen100109" osisID="Mark.7.37" type="section"/>

               <ns0:head>CHAP. VII.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 THen came together the Pharisees, and certain of the scribes, which came from Jerusalem</ns0:p>

                  </ns0:note> defiled (that is to say, with unwashen hands) they found fault.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>heir</ns0:hi> hands <ns0:note place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>diligently <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        </ns0:gap>, up <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the Elbow.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> oft, eat not, holding the traditions of the elders.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 And <ns0:hi>when they come</ns0:hi> from the market<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> except they eat not. And many other things there be which they have received to hold, <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> the washing of cups, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Sextari<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                        </ns0:gap> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> about a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> and a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> of pots, and of brasen vessels, and of <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or. <ns0:hi>Be<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> tables.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Then the Pharisees, and scribes asked him, Why walk not thy disciples according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with unwashen hands.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 He answered, and said unto them, Well hath Esaias prophesied of you hypocrites, as it is writ<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten, * This people honoureth me with <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> lips, but their heart is far from me.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Howbeit, in vain do they worship me, teach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing for doctrines the commandments of men.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 For laying aside the commandement of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups, and many other such like things ye do.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And he said unto them, Full well ye <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Fru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strate.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradion.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 For Moses said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 20.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. Deu. 5.16.</ns0:note> Honour thy father, and thy mother, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 21.17. Lev. 20.9. Pro. 20.20.</ns0:note> Whoso curseth father or mother, let him dye the death.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 But ye say, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 15.5.</ns0:note> If a man say to his father or mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever thou mightest be profited by me, <ns0:hi>he shall be free.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And ye suffer him no <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ore to do ought for his father, or his mother.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered, And many such like things do ye.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes upon the nine first Verses of the fifteenth of <ns0:hi>Mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thew.</ns0:hi> By the Notions of <ns0:hi>Traditions.</ns0:hi> Our Saviour understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth not such things, as were delivered to them by God in his Law<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but such things as were delivered to them by the <ns0:hi>Elders,</ns0:hi> that is, their <ns0:hi>Rulers</ns0:hi> in the Church in the former times, for <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9. he opposeth <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> to Gods <ns0:hi>Commandements,</ns0:hi> and saith the latter were neglected by their Zeal for the former, to give Countenance to which <ns0:hi>Traditions,</ns0:hi> as the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> would impose upon us to be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lieve, that Christ Communicated some things to his Apostles, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>hey to the Primitive Churches, by Word of Mouth, which ha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> been so Transmitted from Age to Age, so the Jew<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> pretended that God Communicated his Will in some things to Moses, which Mo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses did not publish to the People. And as the former pretend <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Power by Christ left to the Church to determine <ns0:hi>Rituals</ns0:hi>: So the Pharisees (their true Predecessors) pretended a such like po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wer amongst others, besides the <ns0:hi>Divers washings</ns0:hi> mentioned by the Apostle, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 9.10. amongst the <ns0:hi>Carnal Ordinances im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed only until the time of Reformation,</ns0:hi> they had invented ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny other <ns0:hi>Washings,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>sepimenta Legis,</ns0:hi> Hedges to the Divine Law. They <ns0:hi>Washed</ns0:hi> their Hands often, when they came from Market, or before they did eat, not for Decency, and Neatne<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, but out of Religion, lest they should have been defiled by touch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing any Heathens, or any Polluted things, and not their Hands only, but their Pots, and Cups, their Beds and Tables, and <ns0:hi>Bra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sen Vessels</ns0:hi> (as indeed there is no stop, when once Men have passed the Hedge of the Divine Institution,) of which Popery is a plentiful Instance, where it is hard to discern an Ordinance of God in the Rubbish of their Superstitious Traditions. And 'tis very ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servable, that Superstitious Men are always more fond of, and zealous for, the <ns0:hi>Traditions</ns0:hi> of Men in their Worship, then keep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Commandements of God, it is with the <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> more hainous to <ns0:hi>Violate Lent,</ns0:hi> then to <ns0:hi>Violate the Sabbath.</ns0:hi> For a <ns0:hi>Priest</ns0:hi> to Marry then to commit Whoredom. This <ns0:hi>Zeal</ns0:hi> in them ordinarily produceth a neglect, or slight esteem of the plain Commandments of God. So it did in the <ns0:hi>Pharisees, v.</ns0:hi> 9. up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on which our Saviour calleth them <ns0:hi>Hypocrites, v.</ns0:hi> 6. and telleth them this <ns0:hi>Worshipping of God</ns0:hi> was Vain, Sinful, and Idle, and im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pertinent, there was in it a Derogating from the Authority of God, and arrogating of an undue Authority to themselves by their Commands making those things necessary, which are not so, and as commonly it happeneth, when humane inventions are o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver urged, and Multiplyed, some are urged Destructive of the Divine Law, so it was with those <ns0:hi>Pharisees,</ns0:hi> so they had done as to the fifth Commandment (of which we have spoken plenti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully in our Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15, 8.) Our Saviour goeth on, shewing their Ignorance and Blindness, in imagining that any Person could be defiled by Eating with <ns0:hi>Vnwashen Hands.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 15.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> And when he had called all the people unto him, he said unto them, Hearken unto me every one of you and understand.<ns0:note place="bottom">Our Saviours calling all the People unto him, before he spake what next followeth, and his Prefacing that Discourse with. <ns0:hi>Hearken every one of you, and understand,</ns0:hi> Lets us know that what he was about to say, was a point of great Moment, well worth their Learning, and Observation.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 15.11.</ns0:note> There is nothing from witho<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                     <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap> a man, that en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tring into him, can defile him, but the things that come out of him, those are they that defile the man.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:283" />16 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>tth. 11.15.</ns0:note> If any man hath ears to hear, let him hear.<ns0:note place="bottom">The addition of these Words, <ns0:hi>If any Man hath ears to hear, let him hear,</ns0:hi> con<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>irm what I observed before, that our Saviour look't upon what he said as a truth of very great moment, and with all as such a Notion which carnal hearts and superstitious Persons, had no Ears to hear. This great Truth was. <ns0:hi>That a Man in the sight of God.</ns0:hi> (For of such defilement he alone speaketh) <ns0:hi>could be de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filed by nothing but what came from within him.</ns0:hi> How easily would a Popish Doctor have answered this, doth not <ns0:hi>Disobedience to the Churches commands,</ns0:hi> come from within us, our Saviourthere<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore must be understood of such things as <ns0:hi>come from within, in disobedience</ns0:hi> to the Commands of God, such are those which he mentioneth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21.22. for all things that come from within, do not defile the Man. And it is true, that a <ns0:hi>Disobedience</ns0:hi> to the Commands of any Power, whither Civil or Ecclesiastical is a thing which cometh from within and difileth a Soul, if it be a disobedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence in such things, which God hath given them, a Power to Command, but if not, the case is otherwise.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 And when he was entred into the house from the people, his disciples <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 15.15.</ns0:note> asked him concerning the parable.<ns0:note place="bottom">That is concerning this saying of his, which appeared to them <ns0:hi>Dark:</ns0:hi> For a <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> somet<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>mes in Scripture signifieth no more <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 49.4. yet one would think that our Saviours saying was plain enough. But Custom is a great Tyrant. The prejudice they had received from their Superstitious teachers, Blinded them, and lock't up their Souls from receiving true and spiritual Instructions, we see the same thing every day. What an heinous thing do the Blind <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> think it i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to <ns0:hi>eat Flesh</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Lent,</ns0:hi> or on one of their Fish days? never considering by what Law of God any Men are restrained in such things. Our Saviour in the next Words checks their Blindness.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 And he saith unto them, Are ye so without understanding also? Do ye not perceive, that what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever thing from without entreth into the man, it can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not defile him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 Because it entreth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 6.5. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 8.21.</ns0:note> For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, mur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ders.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 Thefts,<ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>Covetous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nes<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>, Wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">23 All these things come from within, and defile the man.<ns0:note place="bottom">Christ checketh his Disciples for understanding things no better Ignorance is more excusable in those who are Strangers to God and Christ, then in those that have Relation to him. In our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viours enumeration of those things which come out of the heart, several things are reckoned up which are the Overt actions of the Tongue, Eye, Hands, but our Saviour saith, all these flow from the heart, for the Actions of the outward Man, are but the impe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rate Actions of the Will, and things past the Imaginations and Understanding, before they come at the Will, to be chosen or rejected. Here are but some Sins reckoned instead of many, for it is true of all our evil Actions, that they are first hatched in the heart, and are first entertained in our thoughts, in our Under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standings, then chosen by our <ns0:hi>Wills,</ns0:hi> and then the bodily Members are commanded by the Soul to the Execution of them. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> reckoneth more then <ns0:hi>Matthew,</ns0:hi> but in both, the enumerations are imperfect, and some Sins are named instead of all. Nothing but Sin defileth the Man, Sin hath its first rise in the heart, and floweth from thence. See further the Notes upon <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15.18.19 <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And from thence he arose, and went into the the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and entred into an house, and would have no man know <ns0:hi>it,</ns0:hi> but he could not be hid.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 For a certain woman whose young daughter had an unclean spirit, heard of him, and came and fell at his feet.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 The woman was a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>Gentile.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> Greek, a Syrophenician by nation, And she besought him that he would cast forth the devil out of her daughter.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 But Jesus said unto her, Let the children first be filled, for it is not meet to take the childrens bread, and to cast <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> unto the dogs.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 And she answered and said unto him, Yes Lord: yet the dogs under the table eat of the childrens crumbs.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 And he said unto her, For this saying, go thy way, the devil is gone out of thy daughter.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">30 And when she was come to her house, she found the devil gone out, and her daughter laid upon her bed.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> recordeth this History with several considerable additions, See <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 15.21. where we have largely opened it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 15.29.</ns0:note> And again departing from the coasts of Tyre and Sidon, he came unto the sea of Galilee, through the midst of the coasts of Decapolis.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="32">32 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 9.32.</ns0:note> they bring unto him, one that was deaf, and had an impediment in his speech, and they beseech him to put his hand upon him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="33">33 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 8.23. Joh. 9.6.</ns0:note> And he took him aside from the multitude, and put his finger into his ears, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 11.41, <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 17.1.</ns0:note> he spit, and touch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed his tongue.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="34">34 And looking up to heaven, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 11.33.38.</ns0:note> he sighed, and saith unto him Ephatha, that is, Be opened.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="35">35 And straightway his ears were opened, and the string of his tongue was loosed, and he spake plain.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="36">36 And he <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 5.43.</ns0:note> charged them that they should tell no man, But the more he charged them, so much the more a great deal they published <ns0:hi>it.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="37">37 And were beyond measure astonished, saying, He hath done all things well, he maketh both the deaf to hear, and the dumb to speak.<ns0:note place="bottom">This History is recorded by <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> only. <ns0:hi>And again departing from the coasts of</ns0:hi> Tyre <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> Sidon. We heard <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24. of his going into those Coasts, some think that our Saviour did not go out of the Jewish country, tho he went to the Coasts of <ns0:hi>Tyre</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sidon,</ns0:hi> which were Pagan Countries, <ns0:hi>he came to the Sea of</ns0:hi> Galilee, <ns0:hi>through the midst of the Coasts of</ns0:hi> Decapolis. That <ns0:hi>Decapolis</ns0:hi> was an Union of ten Cities so called, is plain by the Name, but what those Cities were, and whether they lay on the same side of <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>Galilee</ns0:hi> did, or on the other side of <ns0:hi>Iordan,</ns0:hi> is disputed: most think they lay on the <ns0:hi>Galilean</ns0:hi> side. <ns0:hi>One that was Deaf, and had an Impediment in his Speech.</ns0:hi> Some think that he was <ns0:hi>Dumb,</ns0:hi> but the Word signifies one that spake with difficulty, so as it is likely his Deafness, was not natural (for all naturally Deaf, are also Dumb; we learning to Speak by hearing) besides that it is said after the cure, <ns0:hi>that he spake plain,</ns0:hi> it was probably an accidental Deafness happening to him, after that he could speak. Their be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seeching Christ to put his hand upon him, proceeded from their observation of him very often to use that rite in his healing sick Persons. <ns0:hi>And he took him aside from the M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>titude,</ns0:hi> not seeking his own Glory, and <ns0:hi>Ostentation, and put his finger into his Ears, and spit, and touched his Tongue.</ns0:hi> All these things were <ns0:hi>ex abun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />danti,</ns0:hi> not necessary actions, or naturally efficacious for his cure, but our Lord sometimes used no Signs, or Rites, sometimes these, sometims others, as it pleased him, <ns0:hi>And looking up to Heaven, he sighed,</ns0:hi> pitying the condition of humane nature, subject to so many Miseries, Defects and Infirmities, and saith, <ns0:hi>Ephphatha, that is, be opened.</ns0:hi> By the Word of his Power, he made the World, and by the <ns0:hi>Word of his Power,</ns0:hi> he upholds it, and by the same Word of his Power, he restoreth any lapsed, or decayed part of it. <ns0:hi>He speaks, and it is done. And straightway his Ears were opened.</ns0:hi> Nature obeyeth the God of Nature. Concerning his Charge of them not to publish it, and their disobedience to it, I have had occasion once and again to speak, and must confess I can neither satisfie my self in the reason from my own thoughts, nor from what I read in others. This Miracle hath no other effect than the People, <ns0:hi>Astonishment,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Confession,</ns0:hi> that what he did was well done; which was the common effect of Christs Preaching, and Miracles upon the most.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
